title: Trump Invokes Defense Production Act for Oil as Brent Clears $114 and AI Credit Stress Hits Treasuries
subhead: Houthi advances toward Bab el-Mandeb forced Aramco to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters, pushing Brent above $114 and prompting Trump to declare petroleum refining essential to national defense. Meanwhile a risk-off wave driven by AI debt worries sent the 10-year Treasury to a one-month low of 4.953%, flattening the inflation trade.

sections.heading: Trump Declares Oil Refining a National Defense Activity, Invokes the DPA
sections.body:
On Thursday President Donald Trump signed a memo determining that petroleum production, refining and related activities are essential to national defense, and invoked part of the Cold War-era Defense Production Act, CNBC reported. The move allows the administration to direct financial incentives toward oil and gas projects, pipelines and liquid-fuel storage.

The memo justified the action by citing 'constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations' that make the US unable to deliver those energy services in a timely manner. It named no specific projects. CNBC noted that Vice President JD Vance said last week the administration would use the DPA to expand capacity at a Texas refinery owned by Delek U.S. Holdings, and that Trump signed legislation last year including $1 billion in DPA funding for energy projects deemed critical to national security. The US averaged about 13.6 million barrels per day of crude output in 2025.

The timing is political as much as strategic. CNBC reported that crude and diesel prices have surged since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, with Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries compounding the fuel shortage, and cited a Reuters/Ipsos poll closing Monday showing just 36% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the economy, less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is now using wartime industrial authority to fix an energy price problem it cannot solve through OPEC diplomacy or the release of reserves. It also signals the administration sees the refining bottleneck, not crude supply, as the binding constraint — diesel and distillates are where the shortage actually bites.

sections.heading: Aramco Evacuates Dhahran HQ as Houthis Push Toward Bab el-Mandeb
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on Thursday, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis. Clashes have raged since the Houthis pushed toward Bab el-Mandeb, the Red Sea chokepoint, according to Reuters.

This is a second front, distinct from the Hormuz standoff. In September the Houthis struck four Saudi cities — Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran — wounding 73 people and setting Aramco installations alight, halting operations at some energy facilities, per Reuters and Nikkei Asia. The Houthis declared a naval blockade of Riyadh in July and have kept striking Red Sea shipping since.

The market response was immediate. Brent futures rose about 4% on Thursday to a five-month high, then extended gains past $114 on Friday; US crude traded near $99.80, per ET Now and Business Standard. Brent is up roughly 3% on the week. Separately, Libya's National Oil Corporation told Reuters that a pipeline valve feeding the Zawiya port from the Hamada and Tahara fields had been shut, cutting output — a reminder that non-Gulf supply is also leaking.

On the Iranian side, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told the Financial Times that Iran is fully prepared to defend itself, and President Masoud Pezeshkian said the US cannot expect dialogue while blockading and threatening Iran. Kpler data showed at least 18 vessel attacks in two weeks, and LSEG warned Iran is now targeting tankers beyond Hormuz, into the Gulf of Oman, jeopardising Gulf loadings and ship-to-ship transfers.
sections.whyItMatters: With Hormuz already impaired, the Red Sea route was the workaround. A Houthi campaign aimed at Bab el-Mandeb closes the alternative and turns two chokepoints into one problem. That is why the same barrel count now commands a higher price — the market is pricing the loss of redundancy, not just volume.

sections.heading: AI Debt Fears Push the 10-Year Treasury to a One-Month Low of 4.953%
sections.body:
The more consequential move this week may be in credit, not crude. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.60% on Thursday, its worst session since June, to 26,008.86, while the Dow was flat and the S&P 500 lost 1.21%, Business Standard reported. Asia followed: Japan's Nikkei fell 1.46% and Korea's Kospi 1.98% on Friday.

The trigger was concern over the financing of the AI build-out rather than an inflation shock. Reuters reported that US 10-year Treasury yields hovered near a one-month low at 4.953% after tumbling on Thursday, burnishing the safe-haven appeal of sovereign debt. ING analysts told Reuters they still expect the 10-year to snap back above 5% given inflation, fiscal deficit and AI trends, adding that the risk-off environment 'takes pressure off the Fed to hike next week.'

The underlying stress is visible in AI-linked credit. CNBC reported that CoreWeave's 9.625% bond due 2032 yields about 14.9% and its five-year credit default swaps sit near 1,082 basis points — above the 1,000bp threshold generally read as distress. Oracle's five-year CDS widened to 315 basis points, up 311% year-on-year. Economist David Rosenberg noted that Oracle, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta have issued more than $228 billion of bonds this year and now account for roughly 10% of the global investment-grade market, calling Oracle the 'canary in the coal mine' given its $132 billion of net debt and BBB- rating.
sections.whyItMatters: For the first time in this cycle, the bond market is rallying on a growth scare while oil sits above $110 — the textbook stagflation setup is inverting into something stranger, where AI capex leverage rather than energy is the systemic risk. A single notch of Oracle downgrades would move $228 billion of issuance from investment grade to crossover territory.

sections.heading: Yen and Franc Catch the Safe-Haven Bid; Yuan Hits a Four-Year High
sections.body:
The currency market sorted the risk cleanly. Reuters reported the yen strengthened 0.3% to 156.28 per dollar, its strongest in over a month and up 1% on the week, its best weekly gain since early September. The dollar index sat at 101.52 after touching 101.44 on Thursday, its lowest since the start of the month.

Japan's September core inflation exceeded the 2% target for the first time in nine months, Reuters reported — broadening price pressure that strengthens the case for a near-term hike. A majority of economists polled by Reuters expect the Bank of Japan to hold at next week's meeting and hike a quarter point in December.

OCBC analysts told Reuters the safe-haven beneficiaries differ by risk: AI jitters favour the yen, Middle East tension supports the Canadian dollar and Norwegian crown through oil, and French fiscal stress benefits the Swiss franc. The franc held at 0.8199 per dollar, near a one-month firmest; the loonie firmed past C$1.40.

The outlier is China. Reuters reported the offshore yuan was little changed at 6.6715 per dollar — its strongest level in more than four years — even as the dollar index sits near a three-week low. The euro was flat at $1.122, weighed by French debt concerns that Reuters said have raised worry about other heavily indebted euro-area members. The ECB is expected to hold its benchmark at 2.5% next week.
sections.whyItMatters: A yuan at a four-year high against a broadly soft dollar, while Beijing's export machine faces tariff pressure, points to managed strength rather than market-driven appreciation. That is a policy choice worth watching: it exports disinflation and signals Beijing wants the currency as a stability anchor, not a trade weapon, right now.

sections.heading: India's Oil Bill Surges as the Rupee Slides Toward Record Lows
sections.body:
India is absorbing the energy shock on both the trade and currency sides. Oilprice.com reported India's oil import bill jumped 48% as crude prices soared, with the rupee weakening after Reuters reported a record low of 95.8525 per dollar — a level that feeds directly into import costs, inflation and the Reserve Bank of India's policy room.

The bind is structural. India has been the largest seaborne buyer of discounted Russian crude, so the EU's 18th sanctions package — which cut the Russian price cap from $60 to $47.60 per barrel effective September 3, per RBC-Ukraine — and the US push for secondary tariffs on buyers of Russian oil both squeeze the discount that has cushioned New Delhi's import bill. CNBC reported in September that the US House paved the way for legislation allowing tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil, giving Trump leverage over India and China.

Higher crude plus a weaker rupee is a compounding problem: every dollar of Brent costs more rupees, and every rupee of depreciation widens the current-account gap that the RBI must fund.
sections.whyItMatters: India is the cleanest test of whether the current oil price is an EM balance-of-payments event or just a rich-world inflation annoyance. A record-low rupee alongside a 48% import-bill jump suggests the former, and it puts the RBI in the same corner as Bank Indonesia — defending a currency while wanting to support growth.

sections.heading: Russia's Gold Drawdown Continues; France Stays Above 5%
sections.body:
Two ongoing stories showed no material change but remain the slow-moving fiscal backdrop. Russia's central bank sold gold for a 10th consecutive month in September, cutting holdings by 6.2 tonnes to 72.8 million troy ounces, the lowest since late 2019, per central bank figures reported by The Moscow Times and Kitco — a cumulative drawdown of roughly 62 tonnes since December, the largest since the 1998 default. The sales fund a war budget that energy revenue no longer covers, and Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries have made the revenue problem worse rather than better.

France's 10-year OAT yield remains above 5%, first breached Wednesday, for the first time since 2002. CNBC reported the OAT-Bund spread has hit its widest since the eurozone debt crisis, with French yields now above those of Italy and Greece. RBC BlueBay's Mike Bell put the political economy bluntly: 'It looks like either the bond markets riot, or the people riot, or both.' Foreign investors now hold nearly 60% of French debt, up from about 48% at the start of 2022.
sections.whyItMatters: Both stories are about the same thing at different latitudes: governments funding deficits by liquidating credibility — Russia in bullion, France in the price of its own paper. Neither has a market solution without a political one.

bottomLine: Washington responded to a five-month-high oil price with Cold War industrial authority, declaring refining a matter of national defense on the same day Aramco evacuated its Dhahran headquarters. The deeper signal, though, came from the bond market: the 10-year Treasury rallied to 4.953% not on peace or OPEC supply, but on fear that AI capex debt — CoreWeave at 14.9% yields, Oracle's CDS tripling in a year — is the fragile link. Oil above $114 now coexists with a growth scare rather than an inflation panic, and that combination leaves the Fed and the ECB with no clean move next week; both are expected to hold. Watch the rupee and the yen, the two currencies where the oil shock is actually being paid for.
sources: Reuters, CNBC, Business Standard, ET Now, Nikkei Asia, CBC News, Oilprice.com, The Moscow Times, Kitco, RBC-Ukraine, ING, OCBC, Kpler, LSEG, EIA
